subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 5! In this unit you will become a confident master of angles and of ruler-and-compass constructions. You already know that an angle measures an amount of turn, and you can name acute, right, obtuse, straight and reflex angles. Now you will learn the powerful angle rules that let you calculate an unknown angle without measuring it at all, simply by reasoning from the angles you already know. This is real mathematical thinking: you will justify every answer with a reason, not just a number.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics 0862 — Stage 8 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Use the rules for angles on a straight line (sum 180°), angles around a point (sum 360°) and vertically opposite angles (equal).
Identify a transversal and the eight angles it makes with two parallel lines.
Apply the corresponding, alternate and co-interior angle rules to find unknown angles, giving a reason each time.
Use the triangle angle sum (180°) and the exterior-angle rule.
Calculate interior and exterior angles of any polygon using (n − 2) × 180° and 360° ÷ n.
Measure and calculate three-figure bearings, including back bearings.
Construct a perpendicular bisector, an angle bisector, a 60° angle, and triangles from given sides and angles using only compass and straightedge.
Set out a clear geometric argument, stating a reason for every step.

concepts.title: The Basic Angle Rules
concepts.explanation:
Before we reach parallel lines, we must be completely fluent with three rules you can use anywhere. These are the building blocks for everything that follows, so learn them until they are automatic.

Angles on a straight line add up to 180°. If several angles sit side by side along a straight line, meeting at one point on that line, their measures add to a straight angle, which is 180°. So if one angle on a line is 130°, the angle beside it must be 180° − 130° = 50°. Angles that add to 180° are called supplementary.

Angles around a point add up to 360°. If several angles meet at a single point and go all the way around it, they complete a full turn, which is 360°. So if three angles around a point are 150°, 90° and an unknown angle, the unknown is 360° − 150° − 90° = 120°. Angles that add to 90° have their own name too – they are called complementary.

Vertically opposite angles are equal. When two straight lines cross, they make an X shape with four angles. The angles that sit directly opposite each other across the crossing point are always equal. We can prove this using the straight-line rule. Suppose two lines cross and one pair of opposite angles are called *a*, with the angle next to *a* called *b*. Then *a* + *b* = 180° because they lie on a straight line. But the angle opposite *a*, call it *c*, also satisfies *b* + *c* = 180° for the same reason. Since both *a* and *c* equal 180° − *b*, they must be equal to each other. That short chain of reasoning is a genuine mathematical proof – notice how each step has a reason.
concepts.example: Let us see the rules working together. Imagine two lines crossing so that one of the four angles is 70°. The angle vertically opposite it is also 70°. The two angles next to the 70° each lie on a straight line with it, so each is 180° − 70° = 110°. The four angles are therefore 70°, 110°, 70°, 110°, and – as a check – they add to 360°, a full turn around the crossing point. Whenever you finish an angle problem, checking that everything adds up correctly is a habit worth keeping.

concepts.title: Parallel Lines and the Transversal
concepts.explanation:
Parallel lines are lines that never meet, however far you extend them. They stay exactly the same distance apart and point in the same direction, like the two rails of a railway track between Nairobi and Mombasa. On a diagram we mark parallel lines with matching arrowheads, and we write AB ∥ CD to say that line AB is parallel to line CD.

A transversal is simply a line that crosses two or more other lines. When a single transversal cuts across two parallel lines, it makes eight angles – four at each crossing point. The wonderful discovery of this unit is that these eight angles are not all different: they come in matching families with beautiful, predictable relationships. Once you know one of the eight angles, you can find all the others.

There are three key relationships to learn. Each has a letter-shape that helps you spot it, but you must always name the rule properly when you write your reason.

Corresponding angles are equal. Corresponding angles sit in the same position at each crossing – for example, both in the top-right corner. If you slid one crossing along the transversal until it lay on top of the other, corresponding angles would land exactly on each other. They trace out an F-shape (forwards or backwards). Because the lines are parallel, corresponding angles are always equal.

Alternate angles are equal. Alternate angles lie on opposite sides of the transversal and between the two parallel lines. They trace out a Z-shape (or its mirror image, an N-shape). Because the lines are parallel, alternate angles are always equal. So if one alternate angle is 65°, its partner is also 65°.

Here is why co-interior angles behave this way. Take a co-interior pair. One of them is equal to an alternate angle of the other (Z-rule), and that alternate angle sits on a straight line with the second co-interior angle. Since angles on a straight line add to 180°, the co-interior pair must also add to 180°. Every rule in geometry can be traced back to simpler rules like this – nothing is magic.

There is a powerful idea hiding here: these rules also work in reverse. If you find that a pair of corresponding angles are equal, or that co-interior angles add to 180°, then the two lines must be parallel. Builders and surveyors use this idea to check that two walls or two roads really are parallel, just by measuring angles.
concepts.example: Let us work an example in words. Two parallel lines are crossed by a transversal, and one angle at the upper crossing is 72°. What can we say about the angle in the same top-right position at the lower crossing? It is corresponding, so it is also 72°. What about the angle between the lines, on the opposite side of the transversal? It is alternate to the 72°, so it is 72° as well. And the co-interior partner of that alternate angle? It must be 180° − 72° = 108°. From a single measured angle, reasoning has given us every other angle in the figure.

concepts.title: Angles in Triangles
concepts.explanation:
The most famous rule in all of geometry is this: the three interior angles of any triangle add up to 180°. It is true for every triangle in the flat plane – tall thin ones, wide flat ones, big ones, small ones. If you know two angles of a triangle, you can always find the third by subtracting from 180°.

We can prove this beautiful fact using the parallel-line rules you have just learned. Draw any triangle ABC. Through the top vertex A, draw a line that is parallel to the base BC. Now the base angle at B is equal to one of the angles at A, because they are alternate angles (Z-rule). In the same way, the base angle at C equals another angle at A, again by alternate angles. Together, the three angles gathered at A lie on a straight line, so they add to 180°. But those three angles are exactly the same as the three angles of the triangle. Therefore the triangle’s angles add to 180°. This is one of the most elegant proofs in school mathematics, and it shows how the ideas of this unit link together.

We can sort triangles by their angles. An acute triangle has all three angles less than 90°, for example 60°, 70° and 50°. A right-angled triangle has exactly one 90° angle, for example 90°, 60° and 30°. An obtuse triangle has one angle greater than 90°, for example 120°, 40° and 20°. Notice that a triangle can never have two right angles or two obtuse angles – there simply is not enough of the 180° to go round.

There is a second, very useful rule about triangles. If you extend one side of a triangle, you create an exterior angle between that extension and the next side. An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two interior angles that are not next to it (the two “remote” or “opposite” interior angles). For example, if a triangle has interior angles of 50°, 60° and 70°, then the exterior angle at the 70° vertex equals 50° + 60° = 110°. As a check, that exterior angle and its neighbouring interior angle of 70° add to 180°, which is correct because they lie on a straight line.
concepts.example: Why does the exterior-angle rule work? The exterior angle and its neighbour add to 180° (straight line). The three interior angles also add to 180° (triangle rule). So the exterior angle must equal the total of the other two interior angles – the two totals of 180° have the neighbouring angle in common, and cancelling it leaves the result. Learning to see *why* a rule is true, rather than only memorising it, is what turns you into a real mathematician.

concepts.title: Angles in Polygons
concepts.explanation:
A polygon is a closed flat shape made of straight sides: triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons and so on. The letter n stands for the number of sides. As soon as you know one simple formula, you can find the angles of a polygon with any number of sides at all.

The sum of the interior angles of a polygon is (n − 2) × 180°. The idea behind the formula is to split the polygon into triangles. Choose one vertex and draw straight lines from it to every other vertex. A quadrilateral splits into 2 triangles, a pentagon into 3, a hexagon into 4. In general an n-sided polygon splits into (n − 2) triangles. Since each triangle contributes 180°, the total is (n − 2) × 180°.

Let us test the formula. For a quadrilateral, n = 4, so the interior angles sum to (4 − 2) × 180° = 360° – which is why the four angles of any rectangle, each 90°, add to 360°. For a pentagon, n = 5, giving (5 − 2) × 180° = 540°. For a hexagon, n = 6, giving (6 − 2) × 180° = 720°. For a decagon with ten sides, n = 10, giving (10 − 2) × 180° = 1440°. The formula never fails.

A regular polygon has all its sides equal and all its angles equal, like the cells of a honeycomb or a well-made floor tile. To find each interior angle of a regular polygon, work out the total and share it equally between the n vertices: each interior angle = (n − 2) × 180° ÷ n. So a regular pentagon has each angle 540° ÷ 5 = 108°, and a regular hexagon has each angle 720° ÷ 6 = 120°. That 120° is exactly why hexagons tile a flat surface so perfectly – three of them meet at a point and 3 × 120° = 360°, a full turn with no gaps.

There is an even simpler idea for exterior angles. Imagine walking all the way around the outside of a polygon. At each corner you turn through the exterior angle, and by the time you return to your starting point you have turned through one full circle. Therefore the exterior angles of any polygon add up to 360°, no matter how many sides it has. For a regular polygon the exterior angles are all equal, so each exterior angle = 360° ÷ n. A regular hexagon has each exterior angle 360° ÷ 6 = 60°, and – as a check – 60° + 120° = 180°, because an exterior angle and its interior angle always lie on a straight line.
concepts.example: This exterior-angle idea gives you a neat way to work backwards. If you know that each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 24°, then the number of sides is 360° ÷ 24° = 15 sides. And if each interior angle is 140°, then each exterior angle is 180° − 140° = 40°, so the polygon has 360° ÷ 40° = 9 sides. Being able to move confidently between interior angles, exterior angles and the number of sides is a key skill for this unit.

concepts.title: Bearings
concepts.explanation:
A bearing is a way of describing a direction using angles, and it is used every day by pilots, ship captains, hikers and surveyors. A bearing follows three clear rules. First, it is always measured from north. Second, it is always measured in the clockwise direction. Third, it is always written with three figures, so we say 060° rather than 60°, and 009° rather than 9°.

Because bearings are measured clockwise from north, the four main compass directions have simple bearings: north is 000° (or 360°), east is 090°, south is 180° and west is 270°. A direction halfway between north and east, which we call north-east, has the bearing 045°. Notice how the whole system is just the angles of a circle, starting from the top and turning to the right.

To measure the bearing of one place from another, you stand at the starting place, face north, and turn clockwise until you are facing the destination; the angle you have turned through is the bearing. Suppose Ibrahim is travelling from Garissa and wants the bearing of Kismaayo. He imagines a north line at Garissa, then measures the clockwise angle round to the direction of Kismaayo. If that angle is 130°, then the bearing of Kismaayo from Garissa is 130°.

A very common type of question involves the back bearing – the bearing of the return journey. If the bearing of B from A is known, the bearing of A from B differs by exactly 180°, because you are now facing the opposite way. The rule is simple: if the original bearing is less than 180°, add 180°; if it is 180° or more, subtract 180°. For example, if the bearing of Kismaayo from Garissa is 130°, then the bearing of Garissa from Kismaayo is 130° + 180° = 310°. If a bearing were 240°, its back bearing would be 240° − 180° = 060°.
concepts.example: Bearings problems often combine with the angle rules from earlier in this unit, because a north line at one place is parallel to the north line at another place – all north lines point the same way. This means you can use alternate and co-interior angles between two north lines to find bearings without measuring. Suppose a ship sails on a bearing of 065° and then turns onto a new bearing of 125°. The angle it has turned through is simply 125° − 065° = 60°, and because the new bearing is larger (more clockwise), it is a turn to the right, that is, to starboard. Reading a bearings problem slowly and drawing the north lines is the secret to solving it.

concepts.title: Ruler-and-Compass Constructions
concepts.explanation:
A construction is an accurate drawing made with only two tools: a pair of compasses for drawing arcs and circles, and a straightedge (a ruler used only for straight lines, not for measuring). These are the tools the ancient Greek mathematicians used more than two thousand years ago, and constructions are still important today because they are exact, they reveal *why* geometric facts are true, and they build careful, patient hands. The golden rule of every construction is: leave all your arcs showing. The faint curves are the evidence of your method.

Constructing a perpendicular bisector. The perpendicular bisector of a line segment is the line that cuts it exactly in half at a right angle. To construct it, open your compasses to more than half the length of the segment. Put the compass point on one end and draw an arc above and below the line. Without changing the width, put the point on the other end and draw two more arcs, so that they cross the first two. Join the two crossing points with your straightedge. That line is the perpendicular bisector. It works because every point on it is exactly the same distance from both ends of the segment – which is why the equal compass widths matter so much.

Constructing an angle bisector. An angle bisector cuts an angle into two equal halves. Put the compass point on the vertex of the angle and draw an arc that crosses both arms of the angle. Now put the compass point on each of those two crossing points in turn and draw an arc in the middle of the angle, so the two arcs meet. Join the vertex to the meeting point of the arcs. That line bisects the angle. If you bisect an 80° angle, you produce two equal angles of 40° each.

Constructing a 60° angle. Because every equilateral triangle has three 60° angles, you can build a perfect 60° angle without a protractor. Draw a base line and mark a point on it. Put the compass point there and draw an arc that crosses the line. Without changing the width, move the point to where the arc crossed the line and draw a second arc that cuts the first. Join your starting point to where the two arcs meet: the angle you have made is exactly 60°. Bisect that 60° angle and you get 30°; construct a perpendicular and bisect a right angle to get 45°. From these you can build many exact angles.

Constructing triangles. You can build a triangle accurately from different pieces of information. Given three sides (SSS), draw the longest side as the base, then open the compasses to the length of the second side and draw an arc from one end, and to the length of the third side and draw an arc from the other end; where the arcs cross is the third vertex. Given two sides and the angle between them (SAS), draw the base, use a protractor to draw the given angle at one end, mark the second side’s length along that arm, and join up. Given two angles and the side between them (ASA), draw the side, construct the two angles at its ends, and extend the arms until they meet. In every case, one important warning applies: for SSS the triangle inequality must hold – the two shorter sides added together must be longer than the longest side, or the arcs will never meet and the triangle cannot exist.

You have now met six connected ideas: the basic angle rules, the parallel-line angle rules, the angles in triangles, the angles in polygons, bearings, and ruler-and-compass constructions. These are not separate topics – they lean on one another constantly. The proof that a triangle’s angles add to 180° uses alternate angles. The polygon formula is built from triangles. Bearings problems are solved with the parallel-line rules, because north lines are parallel. Constructions turn angle facts, like the 60° of an equilateral triangle, into exact drawings. When you see how the ideas fit together, geometry stops being a list of rules to memorise and becomes a single connected story.
concepts.example: The habit that ties everything together is giving a reason for every step. In this unit, an answer without a reason is only half an answer. When you write “x = 110° (co-interior angles add to 180°)” you are doing exactly what engineers, architects and mathematicians do: making a claim and justifying it. Practise writing your reasons in full, and the marks – and the understanding – will follow. Now let us work carefully through some examples together.

methods.title: How to find an angle on parallel lines
methods.example: Two parallel lines are crossed by a transversal. One angle is 118°. Find the corresponding angle, the alternate angle, and the co-interior angle, each with a reason.
steps: Identify the transversal and the two parallel lines.
Decide which family the angle pair belongs to: corresponding, alternate or co-interior.
Apply the rule: equal for corresponding and alternate; add to 180° for co-interior.
Write the answer with its reason.

methods.title: How to find the sides or angles of a regular polygon
methods.example: A regular polygon has 9 sides. Find the size of each exterior angle and each interior angle.
steps: Interior angle sum = (n − 2) × 180°.
Each interior angle = that sum ÷ n.
Each exterior angle = 360° ÷ n, or 180° − interior angle.
To find n from an exterior angle, use n = 360° ÷ exterior angle.

methods.title: How to construct a perpendicular bisector
methods.example: Construct the perpendicular bisector of a line segment AB that is 8 cm long. Describe each step and state how you would check your construction is accurate.
steps: Open compasses to more than half the segment length.
Draw arcs above and below from one end.
Without changing the width, draw arcs from the other end so they cross.
Join the two crossing points — that is the perpendicular bisector.

methods.title: How to construct a triangle from three sides (SSS)
methods.example: Construct a triangle with sides 6 cm, 7 cm and 9 cm using compasses and a straightedge. Check the triangle inequality first.
steps: Check the triangle inequality: the two shorter sides must add to more than the longest.
Draw the longest side as the base.
Draw an arc of the second side’s length from one end, and of the third side’s length from the other.
Join the crossing point of the arcs to both ends of the base.

methods.title: Interior angles of a polygon
methods.example: Find the sum of the interior angles of a regular hexagon, and hence the size of each interior angle.
steps: For a hexagon, n = 6, so the interior angle sum = (6 − 2) × 180° = 4 × 180° = 720°.
Because it is regular, each of the six angles is equal: 720° ÷ 6 = 120°.
Check by adding all six interior angles together — they should total 720°.

methods.title: How to find a back bearing
methods.example: The bearing of a radio mast from a village is 072°. Find the back bearing (the bearing of the village from the radio mast).
steps: The given bearing is 072°, which is less than 180°.
Since it is less than 180°, add 180°: 072° + 180° = 252°.
So the back bearing (village from the mast) is 252°.
Check: the difference between a bearing and its back bearing is always exactly 180°.

workedExamples.title: Angles on a line and around a point
workedExamples.prompt: Three angles meet at a point on a straight line: 47°, x, and 61°. Find x. Then a fourth angle completes the full turn on the other side of the line — find it.
workedExamples.solution: The three angles 47°, x and 61° lie along a straight line, so they add to 180°. Therefore x = 180° − 47° − 61° = 72°. The angles all the way around the point add to 360°, so the fourth angle on the other side of the line is 360° − 180° = 180°, which makes sense because the other side is itself a straight angle.

workedExamples.title: Parallel lines
workedExamples.prompt: Two parallel lines are crossed by a transversal. One angle is 118°. Find the corresponding angle, the alternate angle, and the co-interior angle, each with a reason.
workedExamples.solution: The corresponding angle equals 118° (corresponding angles on parallel lines are equal). The alternate angle equals 118° (alternate angles on parallel lines are equal). The co-interior angle equals 180° − 118° = 62° (co-interior angles on parallel lines add to 180°).

workedExamples.title: Triangle angle sum
workedExamples.prompt: In triangle PQR, angle P = 67° and angle Q = 58°. Find angle R.
workedExamples.solution: The three angles add to 180°, so angle R = 180° − 67° − 58° = 55° (angles in a triangle add to 180°).

workedExamples.title: Exterior angle of a triangle
workedExamples.prompt: An exterior angle of a triangle measures 124°. One of the two remote interior angles is 67°. Find the other remote interior angle.
workedExamples.solution: The exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles, so the missing angle = 124° − 67° = 57° (exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles). Check: the three interior angles are 67°, 57° and 180° − 124° = 56°, and 67 + 57 + 56 = 180. Correct.

workedExamples.title: Interior angles of a polygon
workedExamples.prompt: Find the sum of the interior angles of a regular hexagon, and hence the size of each interior angle.
workedExamples.solution: For a hexagon, n = 6, so the interior angle sum = (6 − 2) × 180° = 4 × 180° = 720°. Because it is regular, each of the six angles is equal: 720° ÷ 6 = 120°.

workedExamples.title: Finding a back bearing
workedExamples.prompt: The bearing of a well from a camp is 048°. Find the bearing of the camp from the well (the back bearing).
workedExamples.solution: 048° is less than 180°, so add 180°: 048° + 180° = 228°. The back bearing of the camp from the well is 228°.

workedExamples.title: Constructing a perpendicular bisector
workedExamples.prompt: Describe the steps to construct the perpendicular bisector of a line segment AB, 10 cm long, and explain how to check the construction is accurate.
workedExamples.solution: Open the compasses to more than half of AB (more than 5 cm). Put the point on A and draw arcs above and below the line. Without changing the width, put the point on B and draw arcs that cross the first two. Join the two crossing points with a straight line — this is the perpendicular bisector. Check: it should cross AB at exactly 5 cm from each end, at a right angle (90°).

workedExamples.title: Setting out a full geometric argument
workedExamples.prompt: Angle a and angle b are vertically opposite, with a = 68°. Angle b and angle c are co-interior angles on parallel lines. Find angle b and angle c, giving a reason for each step.
workedExamples.solution: Angle b = 68° (vertically opposite angles are equal). Angle c = 180° − 68° = 112° (co-interior angles on parallel lines add to 180°).

workedExamples.title: Practice 9
workedExamples.prompt: Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 30°. How many sides has it, and what is each interior angle?

workedExamples.title: Exterior angle theorem: finding all three interior angles
workedExamples.prompt: An exterior angle of a triangle is 115°; one remote interior angle is 48°. Find the other remote interior angle and all three interior angles.
workedExamples.solution: Other remote interior = 115° − 48° = 67°. The third (adjacent) interior angle = 180° − 115° = 65°, since an exterior angle and its adjacent interior angle always sum to 180°. Interior angles: 48°, 67° and 65° (check: 48 + 67 + 65 = 180°, correct).

activities.title: The Parallel-Lines Angle Hunt
activities.materials: paper, a ruler, a protractor, coloured pencils.
steps: Draw two parallel lines using both edges of your ruler, then draw a slanting transversal across them.
Measure all eight angles with your protractor and write each one on the diagram.
Colour each equal pair the same colour: corresponding pairs in one colour, alternate pairs in another.
Check: do your co-interior pairs add up to 180°? Write the additions to prove it.
This activity turns the rules from the Lesson into something you can see with your own eyes.

activities.title: Build a 60° Angle Without a Protractor
activities.materials: paper, a sharp pencil, a straightedge, a pair of compasses.
steps: Draw a straight base line and mark a point near the left end.
Put the compass point on the mark and draw an arc that crosses the line.
Without changing the width, move the point to where the arc met the line and draw a second arc crossing the first.
Join the mark to the crossing point of the two arcs, then measure your angle – it should be almost exactly 60°.
Now bisect your 60° angle to make 30°. You have created exact angles using only arcs and a straight line, just as the ancient Greeks did.

activities.title: The Turning-Bearings Compass Walk
activities.materials: an open space, a real or drawn compass, and a friend if available.
steps: Stand still and face north. Agree that this direction is 000°.
Turn clockwise and stop; ask a friend to estimate your bearing (or estimate it yourself first), then check with the compass.
Call out journeys: “walk on 090°” (east), then “turn to 180°” (south). What angle did you turn through?
For each pair of directions, work out the back bearing and check by walking it.
Walking the angles makes bearings feel natural, the way a ship’s captain feels them.

activities.title: Polygon Angle Investigation
steps: Draw a triangle, a quadrilateral, a pentagon and a hexagon.
In each shape, split it into triangles from one vertex and count the triangles.
Predict the interior angle sum using (n − 2) × 180°, then measure to check.
Make a table of your results and look for the pattern as the number of sides grows.
An investigation like this is how mathematicians first discovered the polygon formula.

activities.title: Construct a Triangle for a Real Design (Family Task)
activities.materials: paper, straightedge, compasses, and a family member or your AI tutor to set the challenge.
steps: Ask a family member (or your AI tutor) to give you three side lengths, for example 5 cm, 6 cm and 8 cm — or choose three yourself if no one is available.
First test the triangle inequality: do the two shorter sides add to more than the longest?
If it passes, construct the triangle with SSS – base first, then two arcs – leaving all arcs showing.
Measure the three angles and check they add to 180°. Then try a set that fails the inequality and see what happens.

activities.title: Tessellation Tile Design (Investigation)
steps: Using the interior angles you calculated, work out which regular polygons meet exactly at a point (angles summing to 360°).
Design a repeating floor pattern, like a masjid or market floor, using squares, triangles or hexagons.
At one meeting point, write the angles and show they add to 360°.
Explain why regular pentagons cannot tile a floor on their own. (Hint: 108° does not divide into 360°.)

After your activities, talk or write about these questions: Which activity made the angle rules clearest to you? Which construction was the hardest to keep accurate, and why? Where in your own home or town do you now notice parallel lines, polygons or bearings? Share your answers with your teacher at your next session, and set yourself one goal for the week ahead.

rules.title: Straight Line, Full Turn and Vertical Angles
rules.text: Basic Angle Rules Angles on a straight line add to 180 degrees (supplementary). Angles around a point add to 360 degrees (a full turn). Vertically opposite angles (where two lines cross) are equal.

rules.title: Corresponding, Alternate and Co-Interior Angles
rules.text: Parallel-Line Rules Corresponding angles (F-shape) are equal. Alternate angles (Z-shape) are equal. Co-interior angles (C-shape) add to 180 degrees.

rules.title: Triangle and Polygon Angle Formulas
rules.text: Triangle and Polygon Rules Angles in a triangle add to 180 degrees. An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles. Interior angle sum of a polygon = (n minus 2) times 180 degrees. Exterior angles of any polygon add to 360 degrees; each regular one = 360 divided by n.

rules.title: Three-Figure Bearings and Back Bearings
rules.text: Bearings Rules Measured clockwise from north, always written with three figures. North 000, East 090, South 180, West 270. Back bearing: add 180 if under 180, subtract 180 if 180 or more.

terms: A line crossing two or more other lines
Opposite sides, between the lines; equal (Z-shape)
Same side, between the lines; add to 180° (C-shape)
Equal angles where two lines cross
Inside a vertex / between a side and the next extension
All sides and all angles equal
Cuts a segment in half at 90°
Cuts an angle into two equal halves
commonMistakes: Always name the rule you used
Check shorter sides sum > longest first

reasoningPrompts.prompt: On parallel lines, two co-interior angles are (4x − 10)° and (2x + 40)°. Find x and both angles.
In triangle PQR, angle P = 2x°, angle Q = (x + 30)° and angle R = (3x − 10)°. Find all three angles.
Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One angle is (5x − 20)° and its corresponding angle is (3x + 40)°. Find x and both angles.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Corresponding angles on parallel lines are equal: 5x − 20 = 3x + 40 → 2x = 60 → x = 30°. So both angles = 3(30) + 40 = 130°.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: The interior angle of a regular polygon is 5 times its exterior angle. How many sides has it?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Interior and exterior angles at a vertex add to 180°, and interior = 5 × exterior, so 6 × exterior = 180° → exterior = 30°. Number of sides = 360° ÷ 30° = 12 sides.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A ship sails on a bearing of 065° for 12 km, then changes course to 125°. Through what angle has it turned, and is it a port or starboard turn?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Turn = 125° − 065° = 60°. Since the bearing increased (became more clockwise), this is a turn to the right (starboard).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Ruler-and-Compass Constructions.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A construction is an accurate drawing made with only two tools: a pair of compasses for drawing arcs and circles, and a straightedge (a ruler used only for straight lines, not for measuring). These are the tools the ancient Greek mathematicians used more than two thousand years ago, and constructions are still important today because they are exact, they reveal *why* geometric facts are true, and they build careful, patient hands. The golden rule of every construction is: leave all your arcs showing. The faint curves are the evidence of your method.
